In mathematics, a '''Maharam algebra''' is a [[complete Boolean algebra]] with a continuous submeasure (defined below). They were introduced by Dorothy Maharam in 1947.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Maharam |first=Dorothy |date=January 1947 |title=An Algebraic Characterization of Measure Algebras |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1969222?origin=crossref |journal=The Annals of Mathematics |volume=48 |issue=1 |pages=154 |doi=10.2307/1969222|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

==Definitions==

A '''continuous submeasure''' or '''Maharam submeasure''' on a [[Boolean algebra]] is a [[real-valued function]] ''m'' such that
* <math>m(0)=0, m(1)=1,</math> and <math>m(x)>0</math> if <math>x\ne 0</math>.
* If <math>x\le y</math>, then <math>m(x)\le m(y)</math>.
* <math>m(x\vee y)\le m(x)+m(y)-m(x\wedge y)</math>.
* If <math>x_n</math> is a [[decreasing sequence]] with greatest lower bound 0, then the sequence <math>m(x_n)</math> has [[Limit (mathematics)|limit]]&nbsp;0.

A '''Maharam algebra''' is a [[complete Boolean algebra]] with a continuous submeasure.

==Examples==

Every [[probability measure]] is a continuous submeasure, so as the corresponding Boolean algebra of [[measurable set]]s modulo [[Null set|measure zero sets]] is complete, it is a Maharam algebra.

Michel Talagrand solved a long-standing problem by constructing a Maharam algebra that is not a [[measure algebra]], ''i.e.'', that does not admit any countably additive strictly positive finite measure.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Talagrand |first=Michel |date=2008-11-01 |title=Maharam’s problem |url=http://annals.math.princeton.edu/2008/168-3/p07 |journal=Annals of Mathematics |language=en |volume=168 |issue=3 |pages=981–1009 |doi=10.4007/annals.2008.168.981 |issn=0003-486X}}</ref>
